utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours, this is case number IT-01-42/2-I, the Prosecutor versus Vladimir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to have the appearances. For the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Phillip Weiner for the Prosecution, seated to my right is David Re, seated to my left is Aleksander Kontic, and to my far left is Sebastian van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence representing Mr. Vladimir Kovacevic, Tanya Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome to you, Dr. Duits. Before we continue our hearing, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And before I will give additional opportunity to the parties to put further questions to you, I would like to raise two issues in relation to your curriculum vitae, which was not yet translated into English when we met last week. The first question is the following. You were appointed permanent forensic expert, it says, in the Court of Appeal of Amsterdam, but I would say it would be at the Court of Appeal in Amsterdam. This raises the question, how you could be appointed a permanent forensic expert in 1991 where your curriculum at the same time tells us that your -- at least that is how I understand it here -- you finished your education as a psychiatrist, I do understand a specialist, a medical doctor specialised in psychiatry only in 1994. Could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's a kind of paradox, but I major already in 1998 and that was under supervision, and in fact, it's a paradox. I am since 1994 psychiatrist but I am already appointed as a permanent expert in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also see in your curriculum that you worked from, on from 1998 as an assistant psychiatrist in the forensic observation and assistance department at the penitentiary institution at Veer, and I know that it is in Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it in the context of that appointment that you prepared expert reports to start with under the supervision, and when you had further developed your expertise, although not yet, to say the full-grown psychiatrist, that on from a certain moment that you were appointed as a forensic expert on the basis of the experience you obtained up till that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I did in the meantime also psychiatric reports and evaluations for court, next to the work in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you do that then independently or also under supervision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Always under supervision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Till I was a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Does any of the parties have any additional questions in relation to this issue raised by the curriculum of Dr. Duits? Ms. Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Duits.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, I just wanted to ask you two questions in regards of your curriculum vitae. Now the first, as I could saw from it, was that -- maybe I'm mistaken, but about 80 to 90 per cent of your work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Radosavljevic, I was about to ask that question, which is in my view a separate question. So -- but if you put it to Dr. Duits, I don't have to do it anymore. Yes, please do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About 80 or 90 per cent maybe of your work, including the articles you wrote, the research you did, the symposia you attended and held speeches on, whereas we can see from your CV in connection with child and adolescent psychiatry. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain way, yes. My research and quality and quality of reporting has a lot to do with adult reporting, but in a certain way you can state that. The quality of research I did on forensic reports has to do also with reports of adults.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just give us an approximate figure, as like did you -- did you do about 50 per cent of your research and your articles and your lectures about child and adolescent or juvenile psychiatry and 50 about adults? Or is it more -- because from the list of all your work that I have seen, I would say that maybe three or four points didn't have anything to do with child, youth, adolescents, juvenile. So I came to the conclusion that at least 80 per cent of your work is connected to youth and juvenile. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my research and my papers, I have, yeah, the main issue is youth. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to that one issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? Due to the assistance of Ms. Radosavljevic, we are already covering at least two issues, the first being education and already being appointed as a permanent psychiatrist and the second one, second issue is the focus of Dr. Duits's work on juvenile and adolescent psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine. Let me just address that second issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Duits, you indicated that the focus of your work or at least your written papers has been juvenile or adolescent psychiatry. Have you also dealt with adults?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes. You can't read it from here, but I have been till -- when was it when I... I think 1998. I worked in prisons as a consultant psychiatrist, from 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just roughly, how many adults have you treated or examined over the years?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. I think, as a correctional psychiatrist, you're a consultant in prison and, for example, in the - how is it translated here? Just a moment. In Veer, which the president called it, that is a forensic observation and -- unit where only very disturbed patients come. And we still do, now, and also I am doing, shifts, supervision shifts for that unit. And also, we do replacements and night shifts for -- because I'm also -- I'm a child and adult psychiatrist but also a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just, when you said you really can't give a number of how many adults you've dealt with?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking about over 100? Over 500?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Over 500. Over 1.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over 1.000?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still dealing with adults to this day?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one additional question in this respect. I see that at symposia you presented a couple of papers on quality of forensic diagnostic assessments. Do I understand that subject well if I would consider it is a methodological study rather than a study focussing on the subject matter of the psychiatric diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you understand the task given to you in this case more in the sense of methodology, or more in the sense of -- or I would say primarily as a methodological question or primary as a substantial psychiatric question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think both. Primarily, you asked. As you -- as I already said last time, that I didn't see the patient myself, and I had to judge on reports, I have to use a method to have an expertise or have a judgment about the quality of the report. And the methods I use is -- comes forward from my own expertise as a researcher on that item, which no one has done in Holland. But I referred also to what the American Board of Psychiatrists has as policy, and also I'm involved - and it's not in my CV - in the development of further policy in -- of general guidelines for forensic psychiatric reporting for the Dutch Board of Psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We stopped last Thursday halfway questions to be put to you by the parties; both parties had a short opportunity to put questions to you. We had this other matter on your curriculum. Ms. Radosavljevic, do you have any further questions for Dr. Duits?

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I have to ask you: Do I have further questions in regards of his CV? Or do I have in general further questions for Dr. Duits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In general, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I took it that you felt free to ask whatever questions you felt free on the CV until now. But if there would be any remaining questions, of course you could include that as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the last hearing that we held in front of the Chamber, I think it was on page 280, you said that forensic psychiatry diagnosis is something different, or as you have expressed it, "something else than psychiatric clinical diagnosis." Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could put this question to you: If you have a patient that is already in a mental institution and that is already or has already, for a period of time, longer time he has been treated, and now you have to do a forensic diagnosis on such a patient, the data obtained from the treating doctors are also relevant for the evaluation of this patient in a forensic sense. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And you have to -- but you have to ask further. You have to corroborate your own diagnostic findings also, the clinical findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. But the doctors are the one who spent a significant more time with the patient than the forensic expert does. So if you don't have time enough to evaluate every aspect -- and it will be hard, it must take over 15 or maybe months to learn mental disturbed person or his way of thinking, then the data that are given by the treating doctors are of great value for the expertise of a forensic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In combination with all of the other factors, of course.

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there is something else. There is a treatment bias. To treat difficult patients you have to be optimistic. And you have to follow your own abatises [sic], and that is something else than respond to juridical questions and to find answers about those questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do agree with me that it's also important to have the data obtained from the treating doctors?

utterances.speaker: NILS DUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I then can go back to our reports, to the reports with which we're dealing. There are going to be some issues that my questions will refer to that would have to do with the specific diagnosis of my client and some issues that we have treated up until now as private, as private issues of my client.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: So I would ask the Chamber if it is possible to go into a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As the Chamber decided before, in the interest of the privacy of the accused, we will turn into a private session when it is necessary to protect his privacy. Mr. Registrar, could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Upon review of the last portion of the private session, the Chamber will decide what portion of the transcript will be made public. As I said before, we have discussed last time a couple of possibilities, how to proceed. I suggest to the parties that they make written submissions in respect of that. The questions are clear, I would say, at this moment. Any comment on this suggestion at this moment? I'm looking to my left, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like me to briefly address the issues at this time, the four issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's close to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Written submissions would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Written submissions. You don't mind? What time would you need to put them on paper. I take it that you prepared them already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One week would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One week would be fine. Ms. Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with my colleague. One week would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you clearly keep in mind that 11 bis issues as such are not of course to be determined by this Chamber, but by the referral bench. If there are no further issues to be raised, we will adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.
